why: the comparison was made and carries no verdict yet
claim: An azimuth byte does not scale an angle and does not have 128 values. Two is added to it, the result is shifted right two places, the centre is taken off, and what is left is stopped at 15 either way -- so the byte reaches 31 positions 12 degrees apart, from L180 through 0 to R180. The added two is the rounding of a divide by four and nothing else: without it every position would sit a byte off the one the page prints. Twenty nine of the positions are 4 byte values wide and the two poles are 6, which is not a widening of those positions but the clamp taking the two values at each end of the byte the shift would have carried past them. The two poles are one place: half a turn to the left is half a turn to the right, and the page writes that into both cells rather than leaving it to be noticed.
whyNotNamed: There is nothing to call it. A shift, a rounding term and a clamp are three lines of whatever the part is written in, and naming them would be naming arithmetic.
adds: The page states a setting at each of the byte's values and says nothing about how one becomes the other. What is added is that it is a shift and not a divide, that the rounding term is two, that the ends are a clamp rather than two wider positions, and that the whole column is 31 positions and not 128. A reader rendering this parameter needs the rule; a reader checking it needs to know which part of the shape was fitted, and none of it was.
refutedBy: A reading of either slot that puts the output somewhere else at any setting: a change between two byte values this rule puts on one position, or no change between two it puts on neighbouring ones, judged against what the same pair of takes says a position differs from itself by. One position out of thirty-one landing elsewhere refutes it, because nothing in it was fitted to be moved.
couldHaveBeenRefutedBy: A sweep of the azimuth byte reading the two outputs against each other at the byte values either side of each of the thirty boundaries this rule puts in, and inside each of the thirty-one runs it puts between them. The rule is wrong if the reading moves inside a position or stands still across one. That run has now been made at every setting of the byte: 30 of 30 boundaries moved, and of 97 neighbouring pairs the rule puts on one position, 5 moved at all and none of them by as much as a tenth of the smallest boundary.
whatItWouldChange: Anything rendering these two types has to put the sound somewhere, and the byte it is handed reaches thirty-one places rather than a continuum. Round it the other way and every position sits one byte off; leave the clamp out and the two byte values at each end of the range land past the pole.

values: Every setting of the sweep beside this whose takes spread by more than 0.05 dB, which is the coarsest its settled settings spread by and the same figure the band reading keeps a band by. The rule reads the takes' disagreement with each other, not the reading's disagreement with anything, so which settings are here does not depend on what the answer turned out to be. Read over every take rather than over the last two: a setting whose last two agree can still have a first take the band reading throws the whole setting away for, and eleven of them did.

eraPriors.claim: A placement of this period is stored as an index into a short table of positions, not as an angle, and the index is got out of the byte with a shift rather than a divide.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: Positions that are not evenly spaced in the byte, or a count of them that is not one more than twice a power of two minus one -- either would say the byte is being divided rather than shifted.

alternatives.reading: The unit does not hold the table its manual prints. What is claimed here is a reading of a page, and a page is the publisher's account rather than the part's.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The sweep. The part holds the table's shape exactly: 31 runs of byte values, 4 wide except the two at the ends which are 6, with every boundary where the rule puts it and none anywhere else. That is not a page's account being repeated, it is a hundred and twenty-seven predictions coming back right.

separatedBy.observable: Where the sound sits between the two outputs, at the byte values either side of each boundary.

predicts.a-byte-rounded-to-a-quarter-and-clamped: 31 positions, moving at 30 boundaries and nowhere else

separatedBy.what_the_run_was: `balance` over the whole byte, 128 settings, two takes each and four at two of them. The stage reads both outputs, which is why it exists; the sentence this alternative carried before -- that no run here could be made -- named a limit of one stage as a limit of the archive.

alternatives.reading: The column is a table of 31 entries the byte's top bits index, written out rather than computed.

separatedBy.why_not_separable: Two ways of arriving at one number differ in where the number comes from and in nothing that comes out. The claim does not rest on the difference: what it states is the thirty-one positions, their spacing and the clamp, and both readings give all three.

alternatives.reading: The positions are the ones measured here and the degrees printed beside them are the publisher's account rather than the part's. The byte reaches thirty-one places and moves between them where the rule says; what is not measured is that they are twelve degrees apart, or that the two ends are behind rather than in front.

separatedBy.observable: Where a listener hears each of the thirty-one positions.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: Not by this archive, and not for want of a stage. What the question needs is a listener: an angle is a fact about where a sound arrives at two ears, and every reading here is a fact about what leaves two sockets. The nearest thing that could be done is to correlate the per-band separation this run published against a head-related set measured somewhere else, which would be a fit of this unit to another measurement rather than a measurement of this unit, and belongs to whoever has both.

comparedAgainst.generatedFrom: The rule as published, with no number in it fitted here or anywhere: the centre, the step and the stop are read off the page's own labels. It is evaluated at every byte value and turned into the one thing a reading between two channels can check -- which pairs of neighbouring settings must differ and which must not.
